question: Tell me about a time you realized you were over-engineering a product because you kept deferring to customer input rather than making a call yourself. What did you do?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first feature, three customers asked for extra config toggles in the dashboard. I kept adding them until the PM flagged scope creep. I realized I was deferring instead of deciding what actually helped adoption.
I pulled usage data, saw only one toggle was used, and proposed shipping without the rest. My mentor agreed and I communicated the decision back to the customers with the data.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you realized you were over-engineering a product because you kept deferring to customer input rather than making a call yourself. What did you do?
Situation: First feature, three customers requested config toggles
Action: Reviewed usage data, proposed cutting unused toggles
Outcome: Shipped simpler version; customers accepted with data explanation
Quote: "I kept adding them until the PM flagged scope creep"
Follow-up: How did you handle the customers who asked? "I emailed each with the usage numbers and offered a future iteration if needed"
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Customer success is our success. The candidate owned an individual feature and stopped deferring after seeing data. "I kept adding them until the PM flagged scope creep" shows self-awareness at junior scope. They used usage metrics to decide, shipped a simpler version, and explained the choice to customers. This demonstrates coachability and local ownership without over-relying on every input. Biggest strength: turned feedback into a data-driven cut rather than endless iteration.

lowerTranscript.text: A customer wanted five new filters so I kept building them into the report. Later we saw low usage but I didn't want to disappoint them so I left the code in.
Did you ever decide to remove any?
Not really, I just asked the customer again and they said they might use them later so I moved on to the next request.

This reflects passive execution rather than learning to balance input with impact at the individual level. Biggest gap: absence of any attempt to cut scope or use data to drive a choice.

raiseTranscript.text: Three enterprise accounts pushed for advanced workflow approvals. I kept queuing the requests until cross-team usage showed 4% adoption. I called a meeting with the accounts team and proposed a lighter v1 that met 80% of needs.
Two accepted after seeing the adoption data; the third escalated but I aligned with the product director and we held the line while offering a custom pilot later.

We added two more integrations that quarter and support load went up, but I didn't revisit the original scope decision.

raiseTranscript.text: Our customer advisory board kept requesting niche vertical features. After two quarters of roadmap drift I commissioned an internal analysis showing these features drove <3% of expansion revenue. I reset the board charter to focus on outcome metrics instead of feature lists.
We reduced vertical feature commits by 40% that year and reallocated two teams to core retention work, lifting net revenue retention by 6 points.
